title: The 1986-1995 agricultural adjustment programme (PASA) removed most input subsidies but left administered wheat prices and the state offices' dual role in place

excerpt: Tunisia's agricultural structural adjustment programme (PASA, also MTASAP) ran from 1986 to about 1995 with two World Bank sector adjustment loans. It cut the input and credit subsidies that the state had paid through…

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content: Tunisia's agricultural structural adjustment programme (PASA, also MTASAP) ran from 1986 to about 1995 with two World Bank sector adjustment loans (SRC-TG-920, SRC-TG-921). It cut the input and credit subsidies that the state had paid through the Caisse Générale de Compensation: CGC-financed input subsidies fell from TND 73 million in 1989 to under TND 15 million in 1993 (SRC-TG-921). Fertiliser, seed, herbicide and most feed subsidies were removed, and real fertiliser prices rose about 6% a year over 1986-1992 (SRC-TG-921). The other half of the programme, ending administered prices and opening the state offices to competition, went much less far: wheat producer prices stayed above the agreed formula and the Office des Céréales kept both a commercial and a regulatory role (SRC-TG-921). The programme is the origin of today's mixed system: fertiliser, seed and most feed subsidies were removed in 1991-1993, while cereals, milk and some other products kept administered prices and state marketing. By 2008-09 input subsidies went mainly to fuel, milk collection premia and irrigation (SRC-TG-710).

sections.heading: Root causes
sections.content:
**Before 1986 (symptom: low private investment; cause: implicit taxation).** At the time ASAL I was designed, output and input prices were fixed below world prices on a cost-plus basis, and agriculture faced "negative protection rates" and worsening terms of trade with industry, which deterred private investment (SRC-TG-920). The PCR reports 1980-85 cereal NPCs of 0.89 (durum), 0.98 (bread wheat) and 0.82 (barley), but does not state their price base. Annex 2 Table 1 gives actual to import-equivalent ratios of 0.75, 0.76 and 0.86 for durum in 1982/83 to 1984/85, which are different numbers from the 0.89 cited in the text; by 1985/86, the ratios were 1.16 for durum, 1.18 for bread wheat and 1.16 for barley. The 1988 value (1.04 for durum) is reported without a stated base either, so the 1980-85 to 1988 comparison may not be like for like (SRC-TG-920).

**The 1986 decision.** Under balance-of-payments and employment imbalances and pressure from international financial institutions, Tunisia adopted a structural adjustment plan from late 1986 with a large agricultural component (SRC-TG-922). Its stated aim was to bring producer prices to world levels with slight protection for "strategic" products, liberalise marketing and phase out production subsidies (SRC-TG-922).

**Asymmetric implementation.** Producer prices for cereals were raised quickly (durum +12.6% real in 1987 and +8.3% in 1988), so that by late 1987, when world grain prices fell, NPCs against actual world prices reached 1.37 for durum wheat (SRC-TG-920). The Bank's completion report notes that implicit taxation had turned into over-protection (SRC-TG-920). Input subsidies were then removed under ASAL II (SRC-TG-921). ASAL II's fiscal objectives were met. The structural objectives were not: only three private firms entered cereals collection, and privatising Office des Céréales centres failed because buyers had to keep all existing staff (SRC-TG-921). El Louhoum kept fixed-price purchasing and import privileges for beef, and the ONH's role in olive oil exports stayed ambiguous (SRC-TG-921).

**A known trade-off.** The Bank's own pre-appraisal analysis showed the ASAL II measures would produce "marginally negative" sector growth and farm incomes. This was not presented in the President's Report, so as not to lose the Ministry of Agriculture's support (SRC-TG-921).

sections.heading: Evidence
sections.content:
- Pre-1986 prices fixed below world prices, cost-plus (SRC-TG-920, para. 6.11).
- Cereal NPCs: the PCR reports 0.89/0.98/0.82 in 1980-85 and 1.04/1.03/0.90 in 1988; The text does not state the price base of either series; Annex 2 Table 1 gives actual to import-equivalent ratios of 0.75, 0.76 and 0.86 for durum in 1982/83 to 1984/85. 1985/86 ratios were already above 1 (durum 1.16, bread wheat 1.18, barley 1.16). Late 1987 actual-world-price NPCs were 1.37/1.27/1.29 (SRC-TG-920, paras. 6.12-6.13 and Annex 2 Table 1).
- Input subsidies (CGC): TND 73 million (1989) to under 15 million (1993). Fertiliser subsidy TND 20 million to 3 million. Fertiliser subsidies ended for Super 16 (1991), Ammonitre 33 (1992) and DAP (1993); Super 45, about a quarter of volumes, was still subsidised, with a declining subsidy, when the ICR was written in 1996 (SRC-TG-921, paras. 26-27).
- Feed subsidies: TND 49 million (1989) to 4 million (1992-93); maize subsidy ended 1992, soybean meal 1993 (SRC-TG-921, para. 28).
- Irrigation tariffs: about 40% real increase (ICR summary; period and cumulative basis not stated); the body gives average annual real increases of 12% in 1991-93 and about 7% in 1994; average 41 millimes/m3 in 1993, about 63-75% of O&M cost depending on definition (SRC-TG-921, paras. vi, 31).
- Rural credit subsidy budget cut by two-thirds (SRC-TG-921, para. vi).
- No backtracking on subsidy cuts during the 1994 and 1995 droughts (SRC-TG-921, para. 59).
- Income effects: realised price changes alone would have reduced value added by 1.3%; modelled real incomes fell by under 1% a year, except for low-income groups in the north and centre; net incomes of four representative rainfed farms (5-80 ha) were "stagnant at best" for small types and declined for the largest from 1989 (SRC-TG-921, paras. 62-63).

**Disagreement on the fertiliser subsidy end date.** The World Bank's 2014 report says fertiliser subsidies "were discontinued in 1991" (SRC-TG-710). The 1996 ICR shows a phase-out over 1991-1993, with Super 45 still subsidised in 1995 (SRC-TG-921). The ICR is the more detailed, contemporaneous source; both are recorded.

**Disagreement on whether liberalisation was desirable.** The World Bank judged the reforms satisfactory and pushed for more (SRC-TG-921). Boughzala and Elloumi (1992), with a risk-constrained linear programming model, concluded that full liberalisation was not in Tunisia's interest while its main partners (the EEC) protected their own agriculture, and called PASA's liberalisation "timid" because of internal resistance and partners' protectionism (SRC-TG-922).

sections.heading: Why confidence is what it is
sections.content: Medium. The policy chronology and subsidy amounts come from two World Bank completion reports written at the time from government data (SRC-TG-920, SRC-TG-921), which are detailed but are self-evaluations by the lender that designed the programme. Income effects rest on models and four farm budgets, not on observed incomes. One peer-reviewed Tunisian paper gives an independent reading of the programme (SRC-TG-922). No aggregate PSE/NRA series was found to measure the shift from taxation to support across all products (see data_gaps).

sections.heading: Links to other sectors
sections.content:
- **Water.** The programme raised irrigation tariffs by about 40% in real terms (period not stated) and set a target of covering 100% of O&M costs per CRDA. In 1993 tariffs covered about 63-75% of O&M (SRC-TG-921). This is the origin of later irrigation water pricing debates (water lane, theme water-governance).
- **Energy.** By 2008-2009, fuel subsidies were about 40% of agricultural input subsidies (SRC-TG-710). The input subsidy base had moved from fertiliser and feed (cut under PASA) to energy. The causal link to PASA is not established in the sources.

sections.heading: Leads for phase 2
sections.content:
- World Bank Agricultural Sector Adjustment Loans I (Loan 2754-TUN, 1986) and II (Loan 3078-TUN, 1989): https://documents.worldbank.org/curated/en/297621468118154734
- World Bank Agricultural Sector Investment Loans I and II (1993, 1998), which followed the adjustment loans.
- Moving-average world-price formula for setting producer prices (SRC-TG-920, Annex 1).
- Variable levy on milk powder imports targeting 15% nominal protection (SRC-TG-921, paras. 19-20).
- Binomial irrigation tariff decree (1992) and CRDA commercial cost accounting (SRC-TG-921, paras. 30-31).
- Private cereal storage payments (monthly storage premiums), reported as successful (SRC-TG-921, para. 16).

sections.heading: Verification
sections.content:
Programme chronology, subsidy amounts and NPCs were traced to the World Bank text versions of the ICR (SRC-TG-921) and PCR (SRC-TG-920) and local transcripts.

**Independent review, 21 November 2026:** pass after corrections. Checked: SRC-TG-921 ICR summary para. vi and paras. 13, 15, 26-28, 31, 62-63; SRC-TG-920 PCR paras. 1.05, 6.11-6.13 and Annex 2 Table 1 (durum and bread wheat rows opened again; the table gives actual to import-equivalent ratios of 0.75, 0.76, 0.86, 1.16, 1.37 for durum). Corrections: the claim that Annex 2 Table 1 shows the 1980-85 NPCs use import-equivalent prices removed, the report does not state their base; irrigation tariff "40% cumulative 1989-1995" changed to "about 40% real increase, period not stated" with the annual rates of the body added; the year 1995 removed from the cereal-collection and Super 45 statements. Independent teammate sign-off is outstanding; reviewer and author share the TahaGHZ identity, so the record is not validated.

Chapter subtitle, p. 259 (printed):

> Tunisia does not have an agricultural policy; rather it has a food security policy, which goes against the potential of its agricultural sector

Box 9.1 discussion, pp. 261-262:

> not have a strong comparative advantage in cereals, which are intensive in land and are socially less profitable than arboriculture, fruits, and vegetables (box 9.1).

> Tunisia is also competitive in durum wheat (rain-fed and irrigated) and was also competitive in irrigated soft wheat when the international prices spiked in 2008, such that temporarily it became profitable to produce soft wheat in Tunisia. The competitiveness in soft wheat is limited to the irrigated areas and areas in the north and northwest regions where the rainfall is more favorable (not shown).

Section 9.2, p. 263:

> Market price support is carried out mostly through the implementation of a guaranteed minimum price for producers of cereals and intervention purchases carried out by the state marketing boards for milk, sugar beet, and tobacco.

> Cereals (soft wheat, durum wheat, and barley) account for a further third of the expenditure on market price support.

p. 265:

> pays inadequate quality bonuses for cereals, and caps the prices of processed foods.

p. 266:

> In 2009 the budgetary cost of food subsidies was approximately 1.5 percent of GDP, and this amount increased to over three percent of GDP in 2012 (table 9.3).

pp. 267-268:

> it is estimated that the annual cost of protecting employment in the cereals sector is four times the national per capita income.

> The farms that would lose from liberalization are generally those that produce cereals in the better--watered north and northwest parts of the country.

> contrary to popular belief, the agricultural policy does not promote small family farms but mostly benefits a few large land owners (producing wheat, milk, and beef), who are often the most prosperous. This is because most support is provided based on output and farm size.

Additional extracts on Mediterranean and export crops (added for FND-TG-860/861). Page numbers follow the printed page footers, checked page by page:

Chapter introduction, p. 260:

> The current system of state intervention has repressed the agricultural sector, distorting production away from Mediterranean products in which Tunisia has a natural comparative advantage toward continental products in which Tunisia is not very competitive but which are key to food security.

p. 262:

> Tunisia is very competitive in production of olive oil and tomatoes (as shown by the DRC < 1) in each of the three years for which the analysis has been carried out (2000, 2004, and 2008). It is also competitive in production of oranges and potatoes, except in 2008 when the price of fertilizer was extremely high.

p. 262:

> The most competitive products, namely durum wheat, arboriculture (including fruit and olive oil), vegetables, and fisheries--which represent 58 percent of production over the last 20 years--contribute to the growth of the sector only up to about 46 percent, while non-competitive products (cereals, excluding durum wheat, beef, milk)--which concern 39 percent of production--contributed up to about 52 percent (table 9.1).

> in 1998 Tunisia used only approximately 55 percent of its citrus export quota (CNEA 2005b), and this amount was still only approximately 60 percent in 2010 and 2011

> Similarly, Tunisian used only 25 percent of its tomato quota in 1998 and still used only 50 to 70 percent of its quota in 2010 and 2011, respectively. Even for olive oil, Tunisia still manages to export only about 20 percent of its quota.

Box 9.2, p. 264:

> Citrus production has stagnated for more than a decade, and growing domestic demand absorbs more than 90 percent of local production. Current citrus exports to the EU amount to 24,000 tons and represent only 60 percent of the country's preferential quota.

pp. 265-266:

> The focus of farmers on products in which Tunisia is not competitive is the direct result of existing agricultural policies. In fact much of the growth in agriculture has been driven by subsidies and the trade protection of products in which Tunisia is not competitive.

> In 2008-2009, the largest share was allocated to fuel subsides (approximately 40 percent of total input subsidies), milk collection premia (approximately 40 percent), and irrigation subsidies (approximately 18 percent).

pp. 268-269:

> The bias introduced by protection of selected agricultural products results in a reallocation of capital and labor toward those overprotected products at the expense of alternative products in which Tunisia's exports have a comparative advantage, thus introducing an anti-export bias.

Additional extracts on the support framework, budget transfers and simulations (added for FND-TG-920/921/922). Page numbers here follow the printed page footers of the PDF (the footer number closes each page), which may differ by one or two from the page references above:

Chapter opening (p. 260):

> This chapter suggests that Tunisia does not really have an agricultural policy but has instead a food security policy that in fact hinders the development of its agricultural sector. The current system of state intervention has repressed the agricultural sector, distorting production away from Mediterranean products in which Tunisia has a natural comparative advantage toward continental products in which Tunisia is not very competitive but which are key to food security.

Section 9.2, p. 265:

> Agricultural production increased by 67 percent (in value) over the period 1990-2010, but almost one-third (17 percent of the value) originates in bovine beef and milk, in which Tunisia is not competitive.

p. 265:

> Market price support is significant, accounting for over 30 percent of total budgetary transfers to agriculture in recent years [...] Market price support is carried out mostly through the implementation of a guaranteed minimum price for producers of cereals and intervention purchases carried out by the state marketing boards for milk, sugar beet, and tobacco. [...] Market price support is particularly important in the milk sector, which accounts for over 50 percent of expenditure on market price support in recent years. Cereals (soft wheat, durum wheat, and barley) account for a further third of the expenditure on market price support.

p. 266:

> The simple average of the "most favored nation" (MFN) rates applied to agri-food products is 24.6 percent (compared to 16.5 percent for all products), with a maximum rate of 36 percent. "Record prices" (those above 15 percent, according to the World Trade Organization [WTO] definition) account for about 60.5 percent of agricultural tariff lines, compared to 32.5 percent for non-agricultural products.

> Input subsidies (such as improved seeds, forage seeds, energy, irrigation water, and so on) also play an important role and account for approximately 20 to 25 percent of total budgetary transfers in recent years: In 2008-2009, the largest share was allocated to fuel subsides (approximately 40 percent of total input subsidies), milk collection premia (approximately 40 percent), and irrigation subsidies (approximately 18 percent). Fertilizer subsidies were discontinued in 1991.

> the state controls the margins of retail sales of several products, puts pressure on wholesalers to keep their prices low, imports when prices are rising (including for products like vegetables for which there is no guaranteed price), pays inadequate quality bonuses for cereals, and caps the prices of processed foods.

> The budgetary direct costs of policies reached approximately 0.8 percent of GDP in 2010 (or TND 350 million) [...] although Tunisia committed (in the framework of the 1994 Uruguay Round of trade negotiations) to reduce the overall mass of domestic support (from 76 million to 66 million dollars), in fact the budget expenditure for agricultural support has been steadily increasing [...] Between 2000 and 2009 the share of market price support and input subsidies increased from 31 to 53 percent while those of investment aid [...] and those intended for general services actually decreased

p. 267:

> the World Bank estimates that the net effect of trade protection of agricultural goods is equivalent to a loss of approximately four percent of consumer spending if the consumer purchases remain constant, and approximately 5.6 percent if consumers readjust their spending in response to changes in relative prices (table 9.4) (for a full discussion of the model and these results see World Bank 2006)

> the elimination of tariff barriers on agricultural products would increase GDP by approximately 0.8 percent [...] However, the elimination of tariff barriers on agricultural goods would also cause a loss of approximately 87,000 jobs from agriculture that would have to be absorbed by other sectors.

Table 9.4 (p. 268), "Effects on the Entire Economy of Opening Up Trade in Agricultural Goods", source CGE model simulations, World Bank (2006). Rows (baseline / full liberalisation with EU agricultural subsidies / without EU agricultural subsidies):

> Economic growth (% per year, in the years following liberalization) 5.7 / 6.5 / 6.2
> Labor force transferred to other sectors (in thousand jobs) - / 87 / 67
> Gains of adjustment (million TND through 2025) - / 7107 / 4441

p. 268:

> Using a linear programming model [...] the World Bank estimates that nearly 70 percent of farms would gain from the removal of price distortions in the agricultural sector (table 9.5). [...] The farms that would lose from liberalization are generally those that produce cereals in the better-watered north and northwest parts of the country.

p. 269:

> contrary to popular belief, the agricultural policy does not promote small family farms but mostly benefits a few large land owners (producing wheat, milk, and beef), who are often the most prosperous. This is because most support is provided based on output and farm size.

> Agricultural producers who operate in filieres (sectors) that hold great promise (for example, dried fruit, olive oil, fruit, and vegetables), prevalently in interior regions, often receive little or no support from agricultural policies and have great difficulty in accessing financing, inputs, information, or advice

Box 9.3 (p. 270), farmer testimony:

> despite the recognized quality of its olive oil, Tunisia is still using only 20 percent of its quota of exports to the European Union.

Recommendations section (pp. 273-274):

> (a) Progressively shift away from price support and orient agricultural policy toward direct income support

> Taking action to improve access to finance for the agricultural sector. Access to finance is especially challenging for investments in arboriculture (olive oil and fruit), which entail several years between the initial investment and the start of the production phase.
resolvedSources.notes: Chapter of the World Bank Development Policy Review published in 2014; underlying analyses date from 2006-2012 (CGE model World Bank 2006; DRC analysis World Bank 2009 using 2000, 2004, 2008 prices). Its view that cereal producers receive market price support contrasts with the 2024 World Bank statement that farmgate prices were below import parity (SRC-TG-705); the two describe different periods and price contexts. The DRC table extracted with shifted values and is not quoted; only prose is used.

resolvedSources.title: Tunisia - Agricultural Sector Adjustment Loan (Loan 2754-TUN), Project Completion Report (Report No. 9308)
resolvedSources.publisher: World Bank, Agricultural Operations Division, Country Department II, EMENA Region
resolvedSources.extracts:
Para. 1.05 (situation before the 1986 programme):

> Within the agricultural sector itself, there were a number of constraints to development. Negative protection rates and worsening terms of trade with other sectors, particularly industry, made agriculture and related support services unattractive for new private direct investment. [...] Support services were controlled to a large degree by the Government. These operations were often inefficient, wasting resources for the economy at large, and frequently resulting in interruptions of supply to farmers.

Para. 6.11 (prices and incentives framework):

> At the time the loan was developed, prices of both agricultural outputs and inputs (fertilizers, improved seed, herbicides and livestock feed) were below world prices and fixed on the basis of a cost-plus methodology. The medium-term program called for linkage with world market prices to be achieved by the end of the medium-term program (1991)

Para. 6.12:

> Output prices for durum wheat, bread wheat and barley were raised by 12.6%, 3.5% and 6.3% in real terms respectively for the 1987 crop year and by 8.3%, 6.7% and 11.4% in real terms respectively for the 1988 crop year. Nominal protection coefficients rose from .89, .98 and .82 for durum, bread wheat and barley respectively between 1980 and 1985 to 1.04, 1.03 and .90 in 1988

Para. 6.13:

> Nominal protection coefficients comparing producer prices to actual world prices were extremely high due to plummeting values for basic grains on the world markets (NPCs were 1.37, 1.27 and 1.29 for durum, bread wheat and barley respectively). [...] At the time, the Tunisians were more concerned about creating incentives for agricultural production than about the budgetary costs of further price increases.

Para. 6.14:

> It was not foreseen at the time that a situation of implicit taxation of the agricultural sector could become one of over-protection.

Para. 6.15:

> Increases in input prices were suspended for the 1989 season due to the severe drought in 1988 [...] Under ASAL-II the Government expects to resume input price increases for the 1990 season and to gradually eliminate all of the input subsidies by 1992.
resolvedSources.notes: Bank self-evaluation of its own loan (ASAL I, approved 1986). Para. 6.12 reports NPCs rising from .89/.98/.82 in 1980-85 to 1.04/1.03/.90 in 1988, but Annex 2 Table 1 shows the bases differ: early 1980s ratios are Actual/Import-equivalent; the formula row begins in 1986/87. Only the 1988 leg is against the moving-average formula. Para. 6.13 compares producer prices to actual world prices of late 1987. These series answer different questions and must not be mixed. The text file is OCR from a scanned original; obvious OCR errors (e.g. "Withie", "resoucces") are corrected above. Cereals-only NPCs; no aggregate PSE/NRA for all agriculture is given.

resolvedSources.publisher: World Bank, Natural Resources and Environment Division, Maghreb and Iran Department, MENA Region
resolvedSources.extracts:
Executive summary, para. iii (reform areas of the Medium-Term Agricultural Sector Adjustment Programme, MTASAP):

> parastatal reforms: divestiture to the private sector of numerous activities of the Cereals Marketing Board (OC), the National Edible Oil Board (ONH) and the Livestock and Pastures Board (OEP) [...] pricing and marketing: adjustment of prices for cereals and milk to keep them more closely aligned with world prices, the introduction of more market driven prices for beef, the reduction of input subsidies, and the liberalization of meat and milk imports

Para. v:

> an analysis prepared by the Bank before appraisal [...] made it clear that the fiscal balance and sector efficiency measures sought under the ASAL II would result in marginally negative sector growth and incomes for farmers. The President's Report did not present these results because of concern that doing so would weaken the support of the key constituency for the Loan, the Ministry of Agriculture (MOA)

Para. vi:

> The Loan achieved its fiscal objectives since budget costs of subsidies for inputs and credit were substantially reduced -- from 73 to 15 million DT for inputs financed through the General Compensation Fund, through a 40 percent real increase in irrigation tariffs, and a reduction by two-thirds of budget allocations to finance rural credit subsidies [...] Parastatal reform was generally successful in disengaging the organizations from non-core activities, but much less so in achieving greater efficiency through increasing competition from the private sector on a more level playing field, particularly for domestic cereals collection and beef imports [...] wheats continue to be overprotected by restrictive import policy.

Para. 13 (cereals collection):

> in practice very little progress is evident in transferring cereals collection to the private sector. Only three new private participants in cereals collection have emerged, and their activities have remained limited. Risks remain large as long as the OC retains both its role a direct competitor in grain collection and also regulator of the effort to promote private collection.

Para. 15:

> Administered producer prices for soft and hard wheat remained high compared with the agreed formula, while barley producer prices have tracked the formula more closely.

Para. 26:

> The inputs involved were fertilizers, animal feeds, improved cereals seeds, seed potatoes and the herbicide 2-4-D. This objective was fully met, with subsidies either substantially reduced or eliminated. The CGC is the financing mechanism for these subsidies, which peaked at DT 73 million in the drought of 1989 but fell below DT 15 million by 1993.

Para. 27:

> Subsidies for three of the four principal types of fertilizer used in Tunisia have been eliminated. Subsidy reduction began with freeing distribution margins with the 1987/88 campaign, and since 1991 by removal of remaining product subsidies (1991 for Super 16, 1992 for Ammonitre 33, and 1993 for DAP). Only Super 45, which accounts for roughly one-quarter of the total quantities of fertilizer applied, still benefits from a (declining) subsidy. [...] For the 1986-92 period, the increase in real prices of fertilizers averaged 6% annually.

Para. 28:

> Overall subsidies for animal feed peaked in the drought of 1989 at 49 million dinar (current prices) before falling to 4 million dinars in 1992-93.

Para. 13 (continued):

> Transfer of OC facilities to the private sector has proved to be unsuccessful because of the lack of interest linked to a condition in the cahier de charges requiring that all existing personnel be maintained by new management.

Para. 16:

> It eliminated the subsidy for transport cost equalization for cereals, and regarding storage, the Government tested, then implemented an approach for private storage, with the introduction of monthly payments for private storage intended to simulate average seasonal price movements. In conjunction with investment incentives, the promotion of private storage of cereals has proven successful

Para. 18 (olive oil):

> new legislation was passed in 1994 that brought much more extensive liberalization to olive oil exports. [...] Nevertheless, the exporters remain concerned about the ambiguous position of the ONH's which mixes elements of partnership, through provision of services and private sector support, and competition, largely through the ONH's own exports to the European market

Paras. 19-20 (milk):

> a condition of effectiveness was elimination of quantitative restrictions on imports of powdered milk and imposition of a variable levy necessary to provide 15% nominal protection according to an agreed moving average formula. [...] The variable levy was implemented in 1990, and subsequently revised in 1991 and 1993. No adjustments have occurred in the variable levy, or in producer support prices, since 1993.

Para. 23 (beef):

> El Louhoum still accounts for about half of beef imports. [...] In 1994 it was obliged to purchase all live cattle presented to it at a fixed price. El Louhoum continues to benefit from subsidies, does not pay the variable levy on meat imports that the private sector is obliged to pay, and sells its products into its own retail structure with prices that are administratively fixed.

Para. 28 (continued):

> This consisted almost entirely of subsidies on barley, as subsidies on corn were eliminated in 1992 and those on soybean meal in 1993.

Para. 28 (drought feed policy):

> Barley is used to compensate pastoralists for grazing land that is taken out of use during rehabilitation programs, and also small livestock farmers during drought years with the intention of maintaining herd sizes and stabilizing incomes. Corn and soybean meal benefit poultry raisers and also dairy operations, mostly on larger scale farms.

English gloss: the report describes subsidised barley as drought support intended to maintain smallholder herds and compensate pastoralists; corn and soybean meal are used by poultry and dairy, especially larger farms.

Para. 31 (irrigation tariffs):

> The tariffs vary by Region, but averaged 41 millimes /m3 in 1993. This is about 75 percent of the costs of operations and maintenance in the old MOA definition, which does not yet include amortisation and provisioning for repair of civil works and equipment within the perimeter, and about 63 percent of operations and maintenance costs which include these latter components.

Para. 59:

> The sustainability of these subsidy reductions does not seem in doubt: there was no backtracking on the reductions during the subsequent droughts in 1994 and 1995.

Para. 62 (updated multi-market model):

> the realized price policy changes alone would have decreased value added by 1.3 percent [...] there was a small decline, under 1 percent per annum, in real incomes, with the exception of the low income group in the north and center of the country, for whom incomes increased.

Para. 63:

> The DGPDIA has analyzed income trends for four typical farm types ranging from 5 to 80 hectares during the adjustment period. [...] Net incomes derived from the models are stagnant at best for the smaller farm types, and decline for the largest representative farm from 1989 levels.
resolvedSources.notes: Bank self-evaluation, covering 1989-1995. Para. 60 admits monitoring data were largely not collected, so income effects rest on a model and on four representative farm budgets, not on observed household incomes. resolvedSources.title: Libéralisation de la politique agricole en Tunisie et la réforme de la PAC
resolvedSources.publisher: Économie rurale, n° 211, pp. 74-79 (Persée), authors Mongi Boughzala and Mohamed Elloumi
resolvedSources.extracts:
Résumé, p. 74:

> A l'aide d'un modèle de programmation linéaire qui intègre la contrainte risque, nous avons pu démontrer que la Tunisie n'a pas intérêt, dans la conjoncture actuelle, à libéraliser totalement sa politique agricole. Par contre, dans le cas d'une libéralisation réelle des échanges au niveau mondial, la Tunisie gagnerait à libéraliser largement son économie agricole.

English gloss: using a risk-constrained linear programming model, the authors find that Tunisia had no interest, under the conditions of the time, in fully liberalising its agricultural policy; if world trade were really liberalised, Tunisia would gain from liberalising widely.

Introduction, p. 74:

> suite aux pressions des institutions financières internationales, la Tunisie a été amenée à adopter, à partir de la fin de l'année 1986, un Plan d'Ajustement Structurel qui donne une large place dans les réformes au secteur agricole (PASA). Toutefois la libéralisation, entreprise dans le cadre du PASA, reste timide et connaît des lenteurs qui sont dues à la fois aux résistances internes, aux conditions réelles sur les marchés internationaux et à la politique protectionniste de nos principaux partenaires commerciaux.

English gloss: following pressure from international financial institutions, Tunisia adopted from late 1986 a structural adjustment plan with a large agricultural component (PASA). The liberalisation under PASA remained timid and slow because of internal resistance, actual conditions on world markets and the protectionism of Tunisia's main trading partners.

p. 75:

> Ces mesures concernent les prix, les subventions à la production et à la consommation, la libéralisation des circuits de commercialisation et de collecte etc.. Ce plan a pour objectif principal le renforcement des mécanismes de marché et le désengagement de l'Etat des fonctions de production et de commercialisation. Il comprend deux volets, d'un côté une valorisation des prix à la production pour atteindre les prix internationaux (non subventionnés) en gardant en plus une légère protection pour les produits dits stratégiques ; d'un autre côté, il est prévu à la fois une plus grande libéralisation de la commercialisation à l'amont et à l'aval de la production et surtout une réduction progressive des subventions à la production.

English gloss: PASA measures covered prices, production and consumption subsidies and the liberalisation of marketing and collection; its aim was to strengthen market mechanisms and withdraw the state from production and marketing; producer prices were to be raised to (unsubsidised) world levels with a slight protection for "strategic" products, and production subsidies were to be phased out.

p. 75:

> L'agriculture [...] occupe près de 26 % de la population active totale. [...] Elle contribue aussi pour 14 % au PIB.

English gloss: agriculture employed about 26% of the labour force and contributed 14% of GDP (early 1990s).
resolvedSources.notes: Short conference paper (CIHEAM/IAM-M session, November 1991). Useful as an academic Tunisian counter-view to the World Bank's liberalisation case. The model results are summarised, not fully documented in the 6 pages.

relatedItems.title: The state cereal system (Office des Céréales monopoly, decreed prices, CGC subsidies) built in 1962-1971 now strains public finances and blunts market signals
Price support and border protection favour cereals, milk and beef over Mediterranean crops and mostly benefit large farms; whether cereal growers are supported or taxed depends on the year
In a 2012 World Bank study, fewer than one farmer in ten borrowed from banks while about a quarter were barred by old arrears; repeated debt write-offs since 1999 have not broken the cycle

The dairy sector built in the 1990s on imported Holstein cows and imported concentrates is contracting: milk output fell about 16% from its 2021 peak to 2025 and the estimated herd shrinks about 2.5% a year (no census since 2019) after drought and feed price shocks; the ministry and farmers describe a lasting gap between feed costs and the administered milk price, frozen at 1,340 millimes since late 2022 or early 2023
